stories.title: One US dollar now costs 2 million rials in Iran, and here’s what it can buy
stories.summary: Sanctions and the US-Israel war on Iran have left the country’s people unable to keep pace with rising prices as the rial hits a new all-time low. The Iranian rial has fallen to a new all-time low against the US dollar, dropping past 2 million rials to $1 on the free market after Washington launched its toughest sanctions yet in efforts to strangle Tehran’s economy. Iran’s economy has been crippled by decades of US and international sanctions, especially over its nuclear programme – the Iranian rial has crashed and inflation woes are piling up misery for people. The US-Israel war on Iran, launched on February 28, worsened the economic woes for the country of some 92 million people. To understand how much everyday items now cost, Al Jazeera tracked the prices of food, clothing and medicines on the streets of Tehran, comparing them with what the same goods cost in the days before the war. How much do basic necessities cost in Iran? Before the war, 2 million rials could buy about 4kg of tomatoes, half a kilo of chicken and a little less than a litre of cooking oil. Today, the same amount buys about half as much, with the average price of tomatoes increasing by 71 percent, chicken by 74 percent and cooking oil by 177 percent. The price of insulin, the baseline survival for diabetics, has shot up by 642 percent, while essential medicine like paracetamol has become dearer by 93 percent, and baby formula, largely subsidised by the government, has become costlier by 95 percent. The graphic below breaks down the average costs of food, clothing and medicine before the war and on Wednesday. Prices remain highly volatile, and the figures reflect average values. For Iranian families, this has meant changing not only how much they buy, but also what they eat.

stories.title: Syria's main Kurdish force SDF ceases to exist after army merger
stories.summary: Commander Mazloum Abdi announced the SDF's dissolution at the presidential palace in Damascus, ending the existence of the Kurdish-led force that served as Washington's main partner against the so-called Islamic State terrorist group. The Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) dissolved on Tuesday after their commander announced the completion of their integration into the Syrian army, ending the existence of the Kurdish-led force that served as Washington's main partner against the so-called Islamic State group in Syria and once controlled a vast autonomous zone in the country's northeast. "We announce today the end of the mission of the Syrian Democratic Forces and declare, with full responsibility, their dissolution as an independent military force," Mazloum Abdi said in a televised speech at the presidential palace in Damascus, following meetings with President Ahmad al-Sharaa. The SDF was formed in 2015 at US instigation to fight the IS group, drawing primarily on the People's Protection Units, known by its Kurdish initials YPG, the main armed force of Syria's Kurdish community. At its peak, the SDF controlled a de facto autonomous zone across much of northeastern Syria, including significant oil and agricultural land. Turkey regards the YPG as the Syrian branch of the Kurdistan Workers' Party, or PKK — designated a terrorist organisation by Turkey, the US, the EU, the UK and France — and has conducted multiple military operations against it inside Syria. The integration is part of an agreement reached on 29 January, which stipulated a ceasefire and a gradual transfer of SDF-affiliated military and civilian institutions to Syrian state control, including border crossings, oil and gas fields, prisons and camps housing IS detainees. The SDF lost most of the territory it controlled in northeastern Syria to a Syrian government offensive in January before signing the deal. After clashes in Aleppo in December 2025, it had already withdrawn from west of the Euphrates. On 16 January, al-Sharaa signed a decree guaranteeing Kurds' national rights, recognising Kurdish as a national language, declaring Nowruz an official public holiday, and granting citizenship to Kurds previously denied legal status. The US described the broader integration deal as "historic". Abdi said the dissolution marked the beginning of "a genuine transition from battlefields to the fields of construction, and from an era of weapons to an era of peace." He added that political efforts would intensify to ensure Kurdish rights were enshrined in the Syrian constitution.

stories.title: Why we should all get used to high household energy bills
stories.summary: Energy bills may have been a long way from our minds through the sweltering summer. Clothes on a washing line have been drying in minutes. Cold showers have been more tempting than hot ones. But the latest news and forecasts on gas prices will bring a renewed sense of worry and urgency to families, as well as government ministers. Energy prices will rise by nearly 4% for millions of households in October. Even more striking is a prediction from the respected consultancy Cornwall Insight of a further 9% increase at the peak of winter in January. With ongoing volatility in the wholesale gas market sparked by events in the Gulf region, the energy sector says high prices are here to stay. EDF suggests bills will remain "stubbornly high" at their current level at least until the end of the decade. High bills have, and continue to, bite. Energy prices have been central to the cost-of-living squeeze. The typical household's dual-fuel bill is now 70% higher than it was at the start of 2021, before Russia's invasion of Ukraine. That amounts to around £600 more each year than pre-crisis levels, according to industry body Energy UK.

stories.title: Promise of riches: Gold rush in small Kenyan village
stories.summary: In the remote Kenyan village of Cheporor, a recent discovery of gold sent thousands of amateur prospectors rushing to the area in recent weeks. The village now looks like a bustling small town, but is lacking the infrastructure to house these arrivals, posing security challenges.

stories.title: Another ten troops returning to Russia today from captivity — human rights commissioner
stories.summary: Yana Lantratova clarified that the swap process in Belarus is currently being finalized using a ten-for-ten formula
article_sentences: MOSCOW, August 26.
Another ten Russian servicemen will return from Ukrainian captivity as part of a prisoner swap in Belarus, human rights commissioner.
Yana Lantratova told reporters.
"Today, ten of our guys will be brought home," she said.
The ombudswoman clarified that the swap process in Belarus is currently being finalized using a ten-for-ten formula.
On August 24, the Pervy Informatsionny TV channel reported on yet another ten-for-ten exchange of Russian and Ukrainian citizens taking place in Belarus’ Gomel Region.
